title: Well planted
hook: what is well planted can't be uprooted; cultivate it in yourself, then your home and village (Tao Te Ching 54)

segments.voice: Yesterday, weeds in the fields: a shining court beside neglected fields, and the chapter called it robbery. Your line was weeds in the fields. Which field did you tend? Day one thousand one hundred sixteen.

The morning after a big storm, a street looks like a sorting machine went through it. The young ornamental tree out front, the one that looked so tidy, is lying across the sidewalk with a flat pad of roots in the air. Two doors down, an old tree has lost some branches and is otherwise exactly where it was yesterday. Same wind. Same night. The difference was underground, where nobody was looking. Chapter fifty-four of the Tao Te Ching is about that underground difference, and about how far it can reach.
screen: `THE MORNING AFTER A STORM.` → `ONE TREE DOWN, ONE STANDING.` → `THE DIFFERENCE WAS UNDERGROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the planting. James Legge set this chapter as verse, and it opens: "What (Tao's) skilful planter plants can never be uptorn." What is held well, it goes on, won't slip away, and the family's offerings carry on from one generation to the next. Rootedness isn't only about surviving a storm. It's about lasting. Second, the circles. Cultivate it in yourself, the chapter says, and your virtue becomes real. Cultivate it in your family, and it overflows. In your village, it endures. In the state, it flourishes. In the whole world, it spreads everywhere. Notice the order. It doesn't start with the world. It starts with one person, and moves out like rings in a pond. Third, the method. The chapter says to look at a person by way of a person, a family by way of a family, a village by way of a village, and the world by way of the world. How do I know the world is like this, the speaker asks. By this. In other words: look at what's actually there, at each size, and see whether the roots hold. Fourth, a smaller garden. Good intentions often get planted shallow: a resolution on a sticky note, a burst of effort that looks tidy for a week. The first strong wind takes it. The chapter's picture is slower. One good thing, put down deep in one life, until it's there whether or not anyone is watching. Then, without any campaign, it starts showing up at the kitchen table, and then down the street.
screen: `WHAT IS WELL PLANTED ISN'T UPROOTED.` · `YOURSELF, FAMILY, VILLAGE, WORLD.` · `LOOK AT EACH SIZE AS IT IS.` · `ONE GOOD THING, PLANTED DEEP.` · then, large: `CAN NEVER BE UPTORN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plant one good habit deeper. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Don't reach for a new habit. Pick one good thing you already do, even a little: a walk, a kind word at dinner, a few minutes of quiet like this one. Picture it as a young tree. How deep are its roots right now? What would put them one inch deeper? The same time each day. A smaller, steadier version. Doing it on the days you don't feel like it. Choose one inch, and rest with that choice. The bell holds the time.
Well planted. Chapter fifty-four: what is planted well can't be pulled up, and it grows outward from one person to a family, a village and the world. Today's word.
Your line: well planted. Do your one good habit today on purpose, one inch deeper than usual, whether or not anyone sees. Day one thousand one hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter fifty-four as a teaching that change begins in one's own life and widens to family, village and world, and that only what is deeply rooted lasts.

trapdoor: what you thought: well planted is a gardening phrase.
what it means: what's rooted deep in one life lasts, and widens from there to a family, a village and the world.
what a scholar hears: Legge sets the chapter as rhymed verse, and it closes by saying to look at each size, from a person to the world, as it is.
